title: Cap. VI Arg. 2: from the nature of special liberating grace — Augustine
pass_a_gloss: The second argument will be taken from the nature of special liberating grace, and of that which is in fact saving. For as Augustine rightly observed, Predestination is not the preparation of just any grace, but of such grace: and such grace, namely that which is in fact saving, is the effect of predestination. If therefore this grace in the hearts of the elect begets faith, does not find it, then much more election itself, which was the cause of such grace to be given, ought to be purely free, and to depend on no preceding act of the human will, but only on the Divine good pleasure.
pass_b_english: Second argument: from the nature of special liberating grace — grace that is in fact saving. As Augustine rightly observed, Predestination is not preparation of just any grace, but of such grace; and such grace, namely that which is in fact saving, is predestination's effect. If this grace in the elects' hearts begets faith rather than finds it, then much more election itself, the cause of giving such grace, must be purely free — depending on no preceding act of the human will, but only on the divine good pleasure.
source_text: Secundum argumentum desumetur a natura gratiae specialis liberantis, et de facto salutiferae. Nam ut recte observavit Augustinus, Praedestinatio non est gratiae cujuscunque, sed talis gratiae praeparatio: et talis gratia, nempe de facto salutifera, est praedestinationis effectus. Si igitur haec gratia in cordibus electorum fidem gignit, non invenit, tum multo magis ipsa electio, quae dandae talis gratiae causa fuit, pure gratuita esse debet, et ex nullo humanae voluntatis actu praeeunte, sed solummodo ex Divino beneplacito, pendere.
